newsitem.title: UK: Alcoholic drinks set for easier UK budget ride.
newsitem.headline: Alcoholic drinks set for easier UK budget ride.

text.p: British Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown, due to announce a special budget on Wednesday, is expected to hit the tobacco industry hard but give alcohol a fairly easy ride, market analysts said.

"I get the impression that as with the Conservatives, Labour are fairly well disposed towards the problems created by cross-border shopping. So I think they will leave rates unchanged on beer," said Mark Puliekis, analyst at Merrill Lynch.

Due to the effects of cross-border shopping, former chancellor Kenneth Clarke left duty rates on beer and wine unchanged for the second year running in his November 1996 budget. He also cut the duty paid on whisky, gin and other spirits by four percent, equivalent to 26p off a bottle of Scotch.
The cut followed a reduction in Clarke's 1995 budget, the first for 100 years.

A survey from lobby group, the Parliamentary Beer Club, predicted imports would double by the year 2000. It estimated that more than two million pints a day would be crossing the channel by the millennium.
The drinks lobby argued that increased excise duty would mean a loss of jobs, as pubs in the south of England especially, were forced to close by a flood of cheaper imports from mainland Europe.

British duty on a pint of five percent alcohol by volume is 30 pence compared with four pence in France. The lobby also argued that raising excise duty would result in a loss of revenue to the Exchequer by encouraging drinkers to take more so-called "booze cruises" to the Continent in order to buy cheaper drinks.
Clarke raised taxes on alcoholic sodas and lemonades or "alcopops" by more than 40 percent or by between seven and eight pence per bottle, to help reduce their appeal to under-age drinkers.

In May, British home secretary Jack Straw launched an urgent ministerial inquiry into the consumption of alcopops to see what action may be needed to stop underage drinking. Many health bodies dismissed Clarke's last duty increase as too low to deter under-age drinking.
At the time of the last budget, excise duties were expected to raise 38.5 billion stg in 1997/98 for the government.
The main components are petrol and derv at 19.6 billion, tobacco at 8.4 billion and alcohol at 5.9 billion.
On tobacco, Labour has adopted a tough stance on health grounds, pledging to ban advertising, including sports sponsorship and Brown is also expected to raise duty rates.

"One assumes that the Labour party will at least continue the prior Conservative party three percent increase and it could possibly be more severe than that," said Charles Pick, analyst at Panmure Gordon.
"It's just a case of how much the industry will get penalised. All the tobacco companies are psyched up to expect a sharp blow," he added.
In the last budget, Clarke raised duty levels on a packet of 20 cigarettes by 15 pence, by seven pence on a pack of small cigars and eight pence on a packet of pipe tobacco.
